extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, constitutionalists, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing the normative and functional criteria by which constitutions and forms of government (especially Parliamentary vs Presidential systems) are judged. Focuses on features that affect stability, accountability, deliberation, and financial governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive appointment and removability by legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive (the Premier) is to be nominated and removable by the vote of the National Assembly (a Parliamentary Republic feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: France under M. Thiers — appointed by and removable by the Assembly; he 'comes down and speaks in it just as our Premier does' and is responsible to it. This arrangement demonstrates the possibility of a republic where executive and legislative authorities are united and not a distinct attribute of monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary 'rationality' (deliberative temperament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationality defined as 'the power of hearing the reasons of others, of comparing them quietly with one's own reasons, and then being guided by the result' is a mental condition necessary for Parliamentary government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assemblies lack this deliberative temper (e.g., they 'scream' rather than discuss), real discussion and thus Parliamentary government become impossible. The French assemblies (especially post-1848) are cited as examples where this quality was deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly composition must allow steady discussion (limited sectional fragmentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies elected from narrow constituencies with fewer sections of opinion are calmer and more capable of steady discussion than assemblies representing many fragmented sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between quieter pre-1848 French assemblies (elected from limited constituencies) and the disorderly 1848 assemblies; many small sections produce 'irritants and species of irritability' that prevent reasoned debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation must appreciate and check Parliamentary government
rubrics_metrics.description: A functioning Parliamentary government requires a nation that cares for and can check its Parliament; otherwise Parliament will not be held to account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The French peasantry's low average intellect/culture and loyalty to local authority (prefet) made them unable or unwilling to check Parliament, placing a Parliamentary Republic at a disadvantage in France.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution power (ability to dissolve the assembly) as a stabilizing check
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prime Minister's power (or equivalent) to dissolve the Assembly is an important check that prevents constantly mutable Ministries; absence of this power makes policy unmanageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: British Premier (effectively) has dissolution power; M. Thiers did not, so the Assembly could change Ministries frequently without fear of the dissolution penalty, risking caprice and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of alternative respected leaders prevents executive monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of other eminent leaders capable of government is necessary to make removal or change of the executive practicable; monopoly of reputation makes replacement nearly impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Thiers' monopoly of reputation (post-Empire) meant the Assembly could not easily replace him; absence of viable alternatives keeps an executive in place beyond what formal law might suggest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive-party linkage (Premier as party head) ensures reciprocal accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: In typical Parliamentary systems the Premier is brought in and maintained by a party which expects reciprocal support; this party linkage constrains and binds the executive to the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinarily a Premier 'is brought in by a party' and that party requires that as they support him he shall support their policies; when an executive is independent of such a party (as Thiers was), normal party-driven accountability is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government by discussion (public parliamentary debate as defining virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary government is characterized by continual public discussion at each stage of public transactions, enabling the public, through Parliament, to remove or install administrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'distinguishing quality' enables public oversight and policy correction; it contrasts with Presidential systems where public discussion does not necessarily determine government fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation/timing of elections in Presidential systems undermines executive-legislative cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Presidents and legislatures are elected in different ways and at different times, there is often no institutional binding between them, leading to frequent disagreement and disunion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the U.S. example (Lincoln/Johnson era) where executive and Congress became hostile: the legislature and executive 'were all the while trying to thwart one another', showing how separation can produce severe conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary scrutiny as corrective for harmful financial policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary systems, through their discussion and investigative capacity, are better able to expose and correct serious financial errors and bad expedients (e.g., inconvertible paper currency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Legal Tender Act' and the issue of inconvertible paper in the U.S. are used as examples: under Parliamentary debate such a policy would have been 'thoroughly searched into and effectually frustrated' sooner than under a Presidential system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation responsiveness and expertise (timely and appropriate taxation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective government requires timely adoption and implementation of sound taxation policy; Parliamentary systems are more likely to diagnose and act on taxation principles quickly and publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. delay and initial avoidance of direct/internal taxes during the Civil War, then later sudden and sweeping taxation ('Wherever you see a head hit it'), are contrasted with how Parliament would have probed and corrected policy earlier and more prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal policy sustainability vs democratic pressure (surplus maintenance trade-off)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary governments find it difficult to maintain large surpluses due to opposition and public sensitivity to taxation; Presidential systems can more easily maintain surpluses but may do so blindly and injure the economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American ability to keep vast surpluses (post–Civil War) is argued to be facilitated by Presidential structure and economic circumstances; England historically could not maintain comparable surpluses because Parliament and public pressure forced reductions (e.g., abolition of income tax).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional composition: 'Dignified' parts to gain authority and 'Efficient' parts to use it
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful constitution has two classes of parts: DIGNIFIED parts (which win reverence, loyalty, and authority) and EFFICIENT parts (which actually work to govern); both are necessary in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignified parts may not do day-to-day business but 'bring it force' by attracting popular loyalty; efficient parts 'employ that power'. Neglecting dignified elements may undermine the ability to mobilize authority, even if they seem ceremonially useless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors (national character and economic conditions) affect constitutional outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Material and moral characteristics of the nation—such as average education, temper, and wealth—shape how well particular governmental institutions will function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: American relative insensitivity to taxes (due to wealth and abundant resources) made heavy taxation and surpluses more politically tolerable; conversely, low average culture in France and loyalty to local authority undermined parliamentary checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of caprice and continuous ministerial change absent institutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscellaneous assemblies, without proper checks, tend to caprice and may change Ministries frequently, producing instability in governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without the fear of penalties (e.g., dissolution), an Assembly 'would be ready to make it [change] once a month.' The text warns that caprice is the characteristic vice of such assemblies.
